Home/Endoscopic sinus surgery

Endoscopic sinus surgery

Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) opens blocked sinus drainage pathways and removes polyps through the nostrils using a fine endoscope, with no incisions on the face. The aim is better drainage and ventilation, and better access for topical treatment to reach the sinuses.

At a glance

Operating time
1 to 3 hours depending on extent
Anaesthesia
General
Incisions
None externally
Back to work
Usually after about a week
Book a consultation

When is surgery considered?

  • chronic sinusitis lasting more than 12 weeks despite appropriate medical treatment
  • nasal polyps
  • recurrent acute sinusitis
  • fungal sinusitis and some other conditions, depending on assessment

Surgery is usually not the first step. Most patients start with medical treatment, and surgery is considered when that isn't enough.

Diagnosis and planning

Diagnosis is based on symptoms, nasal endoscopy and a CT scan of the sinuses. The CT is essential before any surgery because it serves as the map for the operation.

How is it done?

A thin endoscope is passed through the nostril, the openings of the affected sinuses are widened, and obstructing tissue and polyps are removed while preserving healthy lining wherever possible. It may be combined with septoplasty if a deviated septum limits access or breathing.

Recovery and follow-up

Saline rinses are a core part of recovery, with follow-up visits for endoscopic cleaning in clinic during the first weeks. With nasal polyps, sinusitis is a chronic condition that may need ongoing topical treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of recurrence.

Frequently asked questions

Will my face or nose look different afterwards?

No. The operation is done entirely inside the nose and leaves no external mark.

Can polyps come back after surgery?

Yes, in some patients. That is why follow-up and topical treatment after surgery are part of the long-term plan.

Will my sense of smell return?

Smell improves for many patients with polyps after surgery, but the degree of improvement varies and can't be guaranteed.

Is a CT scan really necessary?

Yes, before surgery. It shows which sinuses are affected and the exact anatomy, which makes the operation safer.
